PHASE 7 · FNP CERTIFICATION REVIEW & CLINICAL INTEGRATION

Week 150 — Lesson 174: Neurologic & Musculoskeletal Clinical Integration Board Review

FNP-level goal: Integrate neurologic localization, symptom timing, pain mechanisms, joint and spine examination, functional impact, medication and life-stage risk, and emergency disposition to distinguish common outpatient disorders from brain-, spinal cord-, joint-, bone-, and limb-threatening disease.

Learning Objectives

  • Recognize acute stroke, subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis, status epilepticus, spinal cord or cauda equina compression, septic arthritis, compartment syndrome, and limb-threatening injury.
  • Localize weakness, numbness, dizziness, pain, and gait dysfunction before naming a diagnosis.
  • Differentiate primary headache from secondary headache, seizure from mimics, central from peripheral vertigo, and mechanical from inflammatory or infectious musculoskeletal disease.
  • Select focused laboratory testing, radiography, CT, MRI, vascular imaging, electrodiagnostic testing, lumbar puncture, or joint aspiration when each answers a clinical question.
  • Apply safe initial management, medication review, rehabilitation, fall prevention, referral, and closed-loop follow-up across the lifespan.
  • Use board-style clues without allowing a familiar pattern to override instability or a dangerous alternative.

Part 1 — The NEURO-MSK Framework

Neurologic and musculoskeletal complaints overlap. Weakness may arise from brain, spinal cord, nerve, neuromuscular junction, muscle, pain inhibition, systemic illness, or medication. Back pain may be mechanical, inflammatory, infectious, malignant, vascular, or visceral. The first task is not to order an image; it is to decide whether the patient's brain, spinal cord, joint, bone, limb, or overall physiology is at immediate risk.

  • N — Name the onset and tempo: sudden, episodic, progressive, positional, traumatic, inflammatory, or chronic.
  • E — Examine and localize: mental status, cranial nerves, motor, sensory, reflexes, coordination, gait, joint, spine, vascular, and functional findings.
  • U — Uncover urgent threats: stroke, hemorrhage, infection, compression, fracture, ischemia, or systemic toxicity.
  • R — Review risks and medicines: anticoagulation, immunosuppression, cancer, infection, osteoporosis, substances, pregnancy, and recent procedures.
  • O — Order discriminating tests: test only when the result can change urgency, diagnosis, or management.
  • M — Manage mechanism and function: pain, inflammation, mobility, prevention, and the underlying disease.
  • S — Select safe disposition: emergency transfer, urgent specialist evaluation, or structured outpatient care.
  • K — Keep the loop closed: reassess deficits, function, medication effects, results, and escalation criteria.

Part 2 — Time Course Is Diagnostic Data

Symptoms maximal at onset suggest a vascular event, seizure, trauma, or sudden mechanical disruption. Symptoms evolving over minutes may reflect migraine aura or ischemia; progressive hours-to-days patterns may suggest inflammation, infection, compression, or evolving stroke. Chronic symmetric progression suggests metabolic, degenerative, toxic, or hereditary disease.

Always document last known well for a possible stroke—not merely when the patient was discovered. Ask what the patient could do before symptoms, what changed first, and whether deficits are still present. A precise timeline can determine eligibility for time-sensitive treatment.

Part 3 — First Decision: Stable or Unstable?

Emergency findings include sudden focal deficit, new inability to speak or walk, acute altered mental status, seizure lasting five minutes or recurrent seizures without recovery, thunderclap headache, fever with meningismus or toxic appearance, rapidly progressive weakness, respiratory weakness, new bowel or bladder dysfunction with saddle anesthesia, an acutely hot joint with systemic illness, an open fracture, absent limb pulse, or severe escalating pain with tense swelling.

Check airway, breathing, circulation, glucose, temperature, oxygenation, and medication or toxin exposure. Hypoglycemia can mimic stroke; opioid or sedative toxicity can mimic primary neurologic disease. Correcting a reversible physiologic threat does not eliminate the need to investigate why it occurred.

Part 4 — Localize Before You Label

  • Cerebral hemisphere: contralateral face and limb deficit, aphasia, neglect, visual-field loss, or cortical sensory findings.
  • Brainstem/cerebellum: diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, crossed findings, severe ataxia, or central vertigo.
  • Spinal cord: bilateral weakness, sensory level, upper motor neuron findings below the lesion, and bowel or bladder dysfunction.
  • Nerve root: dermatomal pain or sensory loss with myotomal weakness and reflex change.
  • Peripheral nerve: deficit in a named nerve distribution.
  • Muscle or neuromuscular junction: often proximal, fatigable, or patterned weakness without a primary sensory level.

“Weakness” must be separated from fatigue, pain-limited movement, imbalance, and fear of falling. Test strength against resistance and compare sides rather than accepting the symptom word as localization.

Part 5 — Acute Ischemic Stroke

Sudden face, arm, or leg weakness; speech disturbance; visual loss; neglect; or severe imbalance should activate emergency stroke care. Record last known well, glucose, anticoagulants, baseline function, and symptom evolution, but do not delay EMS transport for a complete clinic workup.

The 2026 AHA/ASA guideline emphasizes rapid system-based evaluation and preserves time-sensitive reperfusion pathways. Eligible disabling deficits may receive intravenous thrombolysis in an appropriate window, and selected large-vessel occlusions may benefit from endovascular thrombectomy based on vascular and advanced imaging. These decisions belong in a stroke-capable emergency system, not the outpatient office.

Part 6 — Stroke Mimics and Hemorrhage

Hypoglycemia, seizure with postictal deficit, migraine aura, intoxication, functional neurologic disorder, infection, and metabolic disturbance can mimic stroke. Mimics are considered during rapid evaluation; they are not a reason to wait for spontaneous improvement.

Severe headache, vomiting, depressed consciousness, very high blood pressure, or anticoagulant use can accompany intracranial hemorrhage, but ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke cannot be reliably distinguished by symptoms alone. Brain imaging is required before antithrombotic or reperfusion decisions.

Part 7 — TIA Is a Warning, Not Reassurance

A transient focal neurologic deficit may represent transient ischemia even when the examination is now normal. The early risk of completed stroke can be substantial. Determine whether the event was focal, abrupt, vascularly plausible, and distinct from generalized weakness, syncope, or gradually spreading migraine symptoms.

Urgent evaluation includes brain and vascular assessment, rhythm evaluation, risk-factor review, and secondary-prevention planning. A risk score can organize information but should not be used alone to declare a patient safe for delayed follow-up.

Part 8 — Secondary Stroke Prevention Is Etiology-Specific

Prevention depends on mechanism: large-artery atherosclerosis, cardioembolism, small-vessel disease, dissection, or another cause. Antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy are not interchangeable. Atrial fibrillation changes the prevention strategy; carotid disease may require procedural evaluation; uncontrolled hypertension, tobacco exposure, diabetes, lipids, and sleep apnea affect recurrence risk.

Medication reconciliation, adherence, bleeding risk, rehabilitation, swallowing safety, mood, cognition, driving, and caregiver capacity are part of post-stroke primary care.

Part 9 — Headache: Primary vs Secondary

A primary headache diagnosis requires a compatible pattern and no evidence that another process better explains it. Migraine often includes moderate-to-severe episodic pain, nausea, sensory sensitivity, and functional impairment. Tension-type headache is commonly bilateral, pressure-like, and less disabling. Cluster headache causes severe unilateral orbital or temporal pain with ipsilateral autonomic features and restlessness.

Do not allow a prior migraine diagnosis to explain every new headache. Compare the current episode with the patient's established pattern and assess neurologic findings, pregnancy, age, immune status, cancer, anticoagulation, trauma, and systemic symptoms.

Part 10 — Headache Red Flags

Urgent features include thunderclap onset, new focal deficit, altered mental status, papilledema, seizure, fever or meningismus, pregnancy or postpartum status, major trauma, anticoagulation, immunocompromise, cancer, a new headache after age 50, or a substantial pattern change. Headache triggered by exertion or Valsalva, positional headache, and progressive daily worsening also merit targeted evaluation.

Imaging choice depends on the suspected pathology and timing. A normal neurologic examination does not erase a compelling thunderclap history.

Part 11 — Subarachnoid Hemorrhage

A sudden headache reaching maximal intensity within seconds to a minute is a thunderclap headache. Subarachnoid hemorrhage may include neck stiffness, vomiting, exertional onset, brief loss of consciousness, or focal findings, but the initial examination can be deceptively normal.

This requires emergency evaluation with appropriately timed imaging and, when indicated, additional testing. Symptom improvement after analgesia does not exclude hemorrhage.

Part 12 — Giant Cell Arteritis

In an adult age 50 or older, new headache with scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, constitutional symptoms, polymyalgia symptoms, or visual disturbance should raise concern for giant cell arteritis. ESR and CRP can support the evaluation but do not replace the clinical assessment.

Transient or persistent visual symptoms make this an emergency because irreversible vision loss can occur. Treatment should not be delayed while awaiting every confirmatory step when suspicion is high; coordinate urgent ophthalmologic or rheumatologic evaluation and diagnostic confirmation.

Part 13 — Meningitis and Encephalitis

Fever, headache, neck stiffness, altered mental status, photophobia, seizure, or focal findings may indicate central nervous system infection. The full classic triad is often absent, especially in infants, older adults, or immunocompromised patients.

Emergency management includes timely cultures, antimicrobial therapy, and lumbar puncture when safe; selected findings require neuroimaging before lumbar puncture. Do not delay life-saving treatment solely to complete outpatient diagnostic sequencing.

Part 14 — First Seizure: Provoked or Unprovoked?

Confirm the event through witness description: onset, gaze or head deviation, focal movement, stiffening, rhythmic activity, responsiveness, tongue injury, incontinence, duration, and postictal state. Syncope can produce brief jerks, and psychogenic nonepileptic events require careful, nonstigmatizing evaluation.

Search for provocation: glucose or sodium disturbance, withdrawal, intoxication, infection, fever, acute stroke, head injury, pregnancy-related disease, or medication effects. An unprovoked seizure requires evaluation of recurrence risk, commonly including brain imaging and EEG. Immediate long-term antiseizure therapy is individualized rather than automatic after every first event.

Part 15 — Status Epilepticus and Seizure Safety

A convulsive seizure lasting five minutes or repeated seizures without recovery is treated as status epilepticus. Protect the airway, prevent injury, check glucose, time the event, and activate emergency treatment. Do not restrain the patient or place objects in the mouth.

After a first seizure, address driving and occupational restrictions according to jurisdiction, bathing and swimming safety, heights, medication adherence, sleep, alcohol, pregnancy considerations, and rescue planning. Counseling is part of treatment.

Part 16 — Syncope vs Seizure

Syncope is transient loss of consciousness from global cerebral hypoperfusion with rapid recovery. Prodromal warmth, nausea, diaphoresis, prolonged standing, or a trigger supports reflex syncope. Exertional or supine syncope, palpitations, structural heart disease, family history of sudden death, abnormal ECG, or injury raises cardiac concern.

Prolonged postictal confusion, lateral tongue injury, focal onset, or stereotyped aura supports seizure, but no single feature is perfect. Orthostatic vitals, ECG, medication review, anemia or bleeding risk, and targeted testing usually provide more value than indiscriminate neuroimaging for uncomplicated syncope.

Part 17 — Dizziness: Define the Syndrome

Ask whether the symptom is continuous or episodic, triggered by head position, associated with hearing symptoms, accompanied by neurologic deficits, or related to standing and medications. “Dizzy” may mean vertigo, presyncope, disequilibrium, visual disturbance, or nonspecific illness.

Acute continuous vertigo with gait inability, new headache, focal signs, or major vascular risk can represent posterior circulation stroke. Bedside eye-movement testing is useful only when performed by a trained clinician in the correct syndrome; misapplication can falsely reassure.

Part 18 — Peripheral Vertigo Patterns

Brief episodes triggered by specific head movements support benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. Vestibular neuritis typically causes acute prolonged vertigo without hearing loss; new unilateral hearing loss can suggest labyrinthine or vascular pathology. Ménière-type disease involves episodic vertigo with fluctuating hearing and aural symptoms.

Canalith repositioning can treat appropriate BPPV. Long-term vestibular suppressants may delay compensation and increase falls, especially in older adults. Persistent atypical symptoms require diagnostic reconsideration.

Part 19 — Peripheral Neuropathy

Length-dependent polyneuropathy usually begins symmetrically in the feet. Diabetes, alcohol, nutritional deficiency, kidney disease, thyroid disease, medications, toxins, and paraproteinemia are among the causes. Focal entrapment neuropathy follows a named nerve distribution.

Rapid progression, marked asymmetry, motor predominance, autonomic failure, proximal involvement, respiratory symptoms, or upper motor neuron findings are atypical and may require urgent neurologic evaluation. Foot protection, fall risk, cause-directed testing, and medication toxicity matter as much as pain relief.

Part 20 — Acute Progressive Weakness

Ascending weakness, areflexia, autonomic instability, facial weakness, or respiratory symptoms may indicate Guillain-Barré syndrome. Fluctuating ocular, bulbar, or proximal weakness may suggest a neuromuscular-junction disorder. Dysphagia, weak cough, declining respiratory force, or inability to hold the head up signals possible respiratory failure.

Do not wait for profound oxygen desaturation; ventilation can fail before oxygenation falls. Urgent neuromuscular and respiratory evaluation is required.

Part 21 — Tremor, Parkinsonism, and Medication Effects

Describe tremor at rest, with posture, or during action. Essential tremor is usually an action tremor; Parkinsonism includes bradykinesia with rigidity or rest tremor and may affect gait and balance. Drug-induced tremor or parkinsonism can follow stimulants, thyroid excess, valproate, lithium, antipsychotics, and other agents.

Assess function, falls, cognition, orthostasis, swallowing, mood, and medication burden. Sudden-onset movement disorder or associated focal deficit is not typical degeneration and needs urgent evaluation.

Part 22 — Low Back Pain: Most Is Mechanical, Some Is Not

Common mechanical pain is often activity-related and improves over time. Radicular pain follows nerve-root irritation and may include dermatomal sensory change, myotomal weakness, or reflex asymmetry. Routine immediate imaging is usually not helpful for uncomplicated acute low back pain without red flags.

Red flags include cancer history, unexplained weight loss, immunosuppression, fever, injection drug use, recent infection or procedure, major trauma, osteoporosis, prolonged corticosteroid use, progressive neurologic deficit, or cauda equina features. A red flag changes probability; it does not establish a diagnosis by itself.

Part 23 — Cauda Equina and Spinal Cord Compression

New urinary retention or overflow incontinence, saddle anesthesia, bilateral sciatica, loss of anal tone, or progressive bilateral leg weakness raises concern for cauda equina syndrome. Cervical or thoracic cord compression can produce gait change, hyperreflexia, hand dysfunction, sensory level, and bowel or bladder symptoms.

These findings require emergency MRI and surgical or spine evaluation. Do not manage new urinary retention plus neurologic deficits as routine back pain.

Part 24 — Spinal Infection

Consider vertebral osteomyelitis or epidural infection with new or worsening focal back pain plus fever, elevated inflammatory markers, recent bacteremia, injection drug use, immunosuppression, dialysis, or recent spinal procedure. Fever may be absent.

MRI is often required because early radiographs are insensitive. Neurologic deficit, sepsis, or suspected compression demands immediate escalation. In a stable patient without neurologic compromise, microbiologic diagnosis should be coordinated before empiric antibiotics when feasible; instability overrides that sequencing.

Part 25 — The Acutely Hot Joint

Acute monoarthritis is septic arthritis until infection has been reasonably excluded. Risk rises with older age, prosthetic joint, immunosuppression, diabetes, injection drug use, skin infection, recent procedure, or bacteremia. Fever may be absent, and serum uric acid cannot distinguish gout from infection.

Urgent arthrocentesis with cell count, Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis is central when septic arthritis is suspected. Crystals do not absolutely exclude concurrent infection. Delayed drainage and antimicrobial therapy can destroy cartilage and cause sepsis.

Part 26 — Gout and Crystal Arthritis

Gout often causes abrupt severe pain, swelling, warmth, and erythema, commonly at the first metatarsophalangeal joint but also at knees, ankles, and other sites. Calcium pyrophosphate disease often affects larger joints and can mimic infection.

Acute treatment must fit kidney function, GI bleeding risk, anticoagulation, interactions, and timing. Long-term urate-lowering therapy is separate from flare relief and requires indication, dose titration, adherence support, prophylaxis when appropriate, and serial urate monitoring. Do not stop a stable urate-lowering medicine solely because a flare occurs.

Part 27 — Osteoarthritis vs Inflammatory Arthritis

Osteoarthritis typically causes activity-related pain, brief morning stiffness, and bony change. Inflammatory arthritis more often produces prolonged morning stiffness, objective synovitis, warmth, and systemic or extra-articular features. Pattern matters: symmetric small joints, axial symptoms, psoriasis, uveitis, bowel disease, or recent infection refine the differential.

Rheumatoid arthritis requires early disease-modifying treatment to prevent damage. Primary care should recognize inflammatory patterns, address vaccination and comorbidity, avoid chronic glucocorticoid substitution for diagnosis, and arrange timely rheumatology care.

Part 28 — Shoulder and Knee Reasoning

For shoulder pain, distinguish active from passive range of motion, weakness from pain inhibition, cervical referral, instability, and traumatic deformity. Markedly restricted active and passive motion suggests joint or capsular disease; preserved passive motion with painful or weak active elevation may suggest rotator cuff pathology.

For the knee, assess trauma mechanism, effusion timing, weight bearing, locking, instability, extensor mechanism, and hip referral. Decision rules can guide radiography after acute injury, but they do not replace neurovascular or infection assessment.

Part 29 — Fracture and Osteoporosis Risk

Suspect fracture with focal bony tenderness, deformity, functional loss, high-energy trauma, or lower-energy trauma in older or osteoporotic patients. An initially normal radiograph does not exclude selected occult fractures such as scaphoid or hip fracture when clinical suspicion remains high.

A fragility fracture is evidence of skeletal vulnerability and should trigger osteoporosis evaluation, fall prevention, calcium and vitamin D adequacy, medication review, and appropriate pharmacologic planning—not just fracture repair.

Part 30 — Compartment Syndrome and Limb Threat

Severe escalating pain, pain with passive stretch, tense swelling, sensory change, or weakness after fracture, crush injury, bleeding, or reperfusion raises concern for acute compartment syndrome. Normal pulses do not exclude it because arterial flow can persist until late.

This is a surgical emergency. Remove external constriction when appropriate and arrange immediate emergency orthopedic evaluation; do not delay for outpatient imaging or repeated analgesic trials.

Part 31 — Pain Mechanism and Safe Treatment

Nociceptive pain arises from tissue injury; neuropathic pain reflects somatosensory dysfunction; nociplastic pain involves altered processing without a single ongoing tissue lesion explaining severity. Mixed mechanisms are common. Pain intensity alone does not identify the mechanism or urgency.

Use function-centered goals and multimodal treatment: education, activity and rehabilitation, sleep, behavioral support, local measures, and mechanism-matched medication. Account for kidney, liver, GI, cardiovascular, pregnancy, fall, and substance-use risk. Sedation stacking and chronic passive care can worsen function.

Part 32 — Life-Stage and Equity Modifiers

Children: consider nonaccidental trauma, septic joint, osteomyelitis, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, and age-specific stroke or seizure presentations. Pregnancy/postpartum: headache can signal preeclampsia, cerebral venous thrombosis, or hemorrhage; medication and imaging decisions should address maternal and fetal safety without withholding necessary emergency care. Older adults: falls, anticoagulation, osteoporosis, polypharmacy, delirium, and atypical infection increase risk.

Communication disability, language access, rural distance, insurance, mobility, and caregiver capacity influence whether a theoretically sound plan is actually safe.

Part 33 — Board-Style Case 1: Acute Stroke

A 72-year-old suddenly develops aphasia and right face and arm weakness 35 minutes before arrival. Glucose is 112 mg/dL.

Reasoning: This is a disabling, abrupt focal deficit consistent with acute stroke. Document last known well and activate EMS/stroke care immediately. Do not delay for an outpatient MRI, aspirin administration, or observation for improvement.

Part 34 — Board-Style Case 2: Thunderclap Headache

A 46-year-old develops the worst headache of life, maximal within seconds while exercising, followed by vomiting and neck discomfort. The neurologic examination is currently normal.

Reasoning: The onset pattern is a red flag for subarachnoid hemorrhage. A normal examination and partial pain improvement do not make outpatient migraine care safe; emergency evaluation is required.

Part 35 — Board-Style Case 3: Cauda Equina

A patient with severe back pain develops bilateral leg weakness, saddle numbness, and inability to initiate urination.

Reasoning: New urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, and bilateral deficit suggest cauda equina compression. Emergency MRI and spine consultation are required; routine physical therapy is unsafe.

Part 36 — Board-Style Case 4: Septic Joint

A 67-year-old with diabetes has an acutely swollen, hot knee, severe pain with passive motion, and malaise. Temperature is 37.6°C.

Reasoning: Low-grade temperature does not exclude septic arthritis. Urgent arthrocentesis and specialist-directed management are needed. Serum uric acid or a presumed gout history cannot safely rule out infection.

Part 37 — Board-Style Case 5: Central Vertigo

A 70-year-old with hypertension develops sudden continuous vertigo, vomiting, inability to stand, dysarthria, and limb ataxia.

Reasoning: Focal neurologic findings and severe gait failure indicate a central process, including posterior circulation stroke, until proven otherwise. This is not routine BPPV and requires emergency stroke evaluation.

Part 38 — Common Board Traps

  • Trap: Symptoms resolved, so a TIA can wait. Correction: transient focal ischemic symptoms predict early stroke and require urgent etiologic evaluation.
  • Trap: Every headache in a migraine patient is migraine. Correction: compare pattern and screen for secondary red flags each time the story changes.
  • Trap: A seizure means lifelong medication automatically. Correction: identify provoked causes and individualize recurrence-risk treatment.
  • Trap: A normal pulse excludes compartment syndrome. Correction: pulses may persist; pain pattern, swelling, and neurologic findings matter.
  • Trap: Crystals exclude septic arthritis. Correction: crystal and bacterial disease can coexist.
  • Trap: All low back pain needs immediate imaging. Correction: uncomplicated pain usually does not; red flags and neurologic deficits change the pathway.

Part 39 — Final Board-Ready Algorithm

  1. Time it: establish onset, last known well, progression, trauma, and preceding illness or exposure.
  2. Stabilize it: airway, breathing, circulation, glucose, temperature, perfusion, and seizure control.
  3. Localize it: brain, brainstem, spinal cord, root, nerve, muscle, joint, bone, or soft tissue.
  4. Threat-check it: stroke, hemorrhage, infection, compression, fracture, ischemia, malignancy, or toxic-metabolic disease.
  5. Test it selectively: choose the study that changes diagnosis or disposition.
  6. Treat mechanism and function: address cause, pain, mobility, prevention, medication risk, and rehabilitation.
  7. Disposition and closure: specify urgency, result ownership, reassessment, restrictions, and return precautions.

High-Yield Summary

  • Sudden focal neurologic deficit is stroke until proven otherwise; last known well must be documented.
  • Transient deficits may be TIA and still require urgent evaluation.
  • Thunderclap headache, meningismus, papilledema, visual symptoms with suspected GCA, or new focal findings are secondary-headache warnings.
  • A first seizure requires evaluation for provocation, recurrence risk, safety, and driving restrictions.
  • Acute continuous vertigo plus neurologic or severe gait findings suggests central disease.
  • Urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, or progressive bilateral weakness suggests cauda equina compression.
  • An acutely hot joint requires urgent exclusion of septic arthritis.
  • Function, fall risk, medication safety, rehabilitation, and follow-up are part of every neurologic and musculoskeletal plan.

Clinical note: This lesson is educational. Apply current guidelines, local stroke and emergency pathways, state driving laws, patient-specific factors, and specialist collaboration in practice.
